frontmatter_description: Use this micro unit to determine whether a character actually noticed a cue, not merely whether the cue was available to the senses.
title: Attention and Salience
use_when: Use when the question asks who noticed, paid attention to, or ignored a specific cue.
Use when the answer depends on whether information entered the character's attentional focus.
Use when one person saw or heard something but only some characters actually registered it.
Use when the task is to diagnose salience, not perception, memory, or belief.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the only issue is whether the cue was visible, audible, or otherwise perceptually available.
Do not use when the main issue is viewpoint, spatial perspective, or what someone could see from their position.
Do not use when the main issue is whether the character later remembered, forgot, or misremembered the cue.
Do not use when the task is about interpreting what the cue meant, inferring belief, or predicting action from it.
decision_variable: whether the cue entered the character's attentional focus
trigger_checklist: Is the question asking who noticed the cue rather than who could perceive it?
Is there a visible or audible event that some characters may have missed despite sensory access?
Does the scene contrast attended versus unattended information?
Is the answer determined by whether the cue was mentally registered at the moment it occurred?
workflow: Identify the key cue and the target character.
Check whether the scene explicitly shows attention: looking toward it, turning, reacting, pausing, commenting, or being distracted.
Separate noticing from mere exposure: sensory access is not enough.
If attention is uncertain, use only cues of actual registration, not later inference from behavior unless the behavior directly shows noticing.
Return the character who truly attended to the cue, or state that no one did if the cue was missed.

special_case.title: Seen but not noticed
special_case.rule: If a character had perceptual access but was distracted, focused elsewhere, or never registered the cue, count that as not noticed.

worked_example.scene: Two people are talking. A phone lights up on the table. One person is watching the speaker closely. The other is reading a text message on a tablet.
worked_example.question: Who noticed the phone light?
worked_example.answer_logic: The phone was visible to both, but only the person whose attention was on the table is likely to have registered it. The distracted tablet reader did not notice it.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to sensory access if the question is only about whether the cue could be seen or heard.
Exit to spatial perspective if the question is about what is visible from a viewpoint.
Exit to memory if the question asks who later remembers the cue.
Exit to belief or inference if the question asks what the character concluded from the cue.

references.route_signal: Use when the diagnostic question is whether a character actually noticed a cue, not whether the cue was present or meaningful.
hard_boundary: Perceptual availability alone is not attention.
Later recall does not prove initial noticing.
Interpretation of the cue is outside this unit.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not assume noticing just because the cue was obvious to the reader.
Do not infer attention from a later reaction unless the reaction clearly shows initial registration.
common_failure_modes: Confusing attention with inference about intention or belief.
Using viewpoint rules when the real issue is distraction.

minimal_pair.case: Two people sit at a desk; a phone in front of them lights up. One glances over and remarks on it; the other is absorbed in a loud argument and never reacts.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Identical sensory access for both, so the decisive variable is which person's attention captured the cue.

minimal_pair.case: The same two people are at the desk, but the phone lights up behind a closed laptop screen so neither could see it light.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Near miss: the deciding variable is now whether the cue was perceptually available at all, which routes to Sensory Access.

boundary_stress_test: Several characters can see the same event, but only one mentions it immediately.
A cue is fully visible in the room, yet the target character is focused on a different task.
A later statement reveals the character noticed something, but the scene never showed attention at the moment.
references.generalization_note: This skill isolates attentional selection: whether a cue became mentally foregrounded, not whether it was present, interpreted, remembered, or acted on.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: A cue is available to multiple characters, but only one is shown orienting to it or mentioning it right away.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: The question asks who could see or hear the cue from their position, with no attention contrast.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The scene asks what someone later remembers or believes after the cue, not whether they noticed it initially.

notes: Keep the unit narrow: attention only, not perception, memory, or inference.
Treat explicit distraction as strong evidence of non-noticing.
Use this unit when the scene hinges on salience and registration, even if the cue is physically obvious.
core_question: Determine who noticed a key cue and who ignored it
